analysis.summary:
This 34-year-old male presents with a complex, two-layered pattern: acute Liver Qi stagnation superimposed on chronic Yin deficiency. The alopecia areata (patchy hair loss) recurred immediately after a stressful work period, indicating that emotional constraint (Liver Qi stagnation) disrupted an already-fragile Yin and Blood supply to the hair follicles. The insomnia, irritability, and rage reflect the Spirit (Shen) being displaced by Liver Fire (Liver Yang rising unopposed by Yin), compounded by Heart Yin insufficiency. His red face, thirst, hot flashes, and excessive sweating are classic Yin deficiency heat signs—not excess heat, but rather Yin's inability to contain Yang, allowing it to float upward and generate spurious heat (虚热).

The tongue provides compelling evidence: the red body (heat or Yin deficiency with rising fire), stasis at the edges (Qi constraint + blood insufficiency), and thin yellow coating (early/mild damp-heat from Spleen weakness secondary to prolonged stress, but not the thick/greasy coat of phlegm-damp) all align with this pattern. The pulse is diagnostically decisive: wiry/string-like quality reflects Liver Qi stagnation and the tension of chronic stress; slippery quality suggests yin deficiency with mild fluid disturbance or heat; sunken and weak at the chi (kidney) position is the hallmark of Kidney Yin deficiency. This combination rule out simple Liver Fire (which would show a rapid, full, bounding pulse) and instead point to a Yin deficiency with stagnation overlay.

Treatment must address both layers: immediate course of therapy will release Liver stagnation while enriching Yin and cooling heat; medium-term therapy will rebuild Liver Blood and Kidney Yin to restore resilience. Without stress reduction and lifestyle change, relapse is likely when the next work crisis arrives. Hair regrowth typically begins 8–12 weeks after Qi-Blood circulation is restored; insomnia should begin improving within 1–2 weeks if Shen is calmed.

treatment.treatment_method: Acute phase (Weeks 1–4): Prioritize releasing Liver constraint and calming Spirit using a formula that both moves stagnant Qi and nourishes Yin simultaneously (modified Chai Hu Long Gu Mu Li Tang). This prevents worsening Yin by aggressive moving herbs alone. Medium phase (Weeks 4–12): Transition to enriching Kidney Yin and rebuilding Liver Blood using modified Zuo Gui Yin, which consolidates the therapeutic gains. Concurrently, address stress via lifestyle and emotional processing. Acupuncture adjunct (if insomnia does not resolve in 2 weeks with herbal therapy alone) at Shen-calming points. Hair regrowth monitoring begins at Week 6; fine/vellus hair regrowth is normal precursor.

beneficial: Goji Lycium berries (Gou Qi Zi / 枸杞)—nourishes Liver Blood and Kidney Yin, brightens eyes, supports hair follicle nutrition; consume 1 small handful daily in soups, teas, or with congee
Black sesame seeds (Hei Zhi Ma / 黑芝麻)—enriches Liver Blood and Kidney Yin, lubricates intestines, promotes hair growth; toast lightly and sprinkle on oatmeal or congee 3–4× weekly
Sour Jujube seed (Suan Zao Ren / 酸枣仁)—calms Spirit, anchors Shen, enriches Blood, promotes sleep; steep 6–9g in hot water 15 min as evening tea 30–60 min before bed
Mulberry fruit (Sang Shen / 桑葚)—enriches Yin and Blood, calms spirit, known to support scalp health; eat fresh or dried (10–15 pieces) as snack or simmer with congee 2–3× weekly
Duck meat (Ya Rou / 鸭肉) and duck egg (Ya Dan / 鸭蛋)—cool in nature, enriches Yin without adding excess heat, reduces internal inflammation; prepare in congee or soup 1–2× weekly
recipes: Goji and Red Date Congee: Cook 1 cup rice with 2 L water over 45 min, add 2 tablespoons goji berries and 4–5 red dates (pitted) in final 10 min, season with a pinch of salt. Eat warm for breakfast; nourishes Blood and Yin, suitable daily.

Black Sesame and Jujube Tea: Roast 1 tablespoon black sesame seeds lightly in dry pan 2–3 min until fragrant, grind coarsely; simmer 8–10 sour jujube seeds in 1 cup water 10 min, strain, pour over sesame powder, add 1 teaspoon honey if desired. Drink warm 30–60 min before bed for 4–5 nights per week; calms Shen and promotes sleep.

foods_to_avoid: Alcohol in any form (beer, wine, spirits)—heats and stagnates Liver Qi, worsens irritability, disrupts sleep quality; eliminate completely or limit to rare social occasions only
Spicy foods and chili peppers—aggravate Liver heat, deplete Yin fluids, increase irritability and insomnia; avoid curry, hot sauce, wasabi, and excessive black pepper
Fried and oily foods (deep-fried snacks, fatty meats, fried rice)—create damp-heat internally, block Qi flow, disrupt Spleen function; remove or minimize to 1–2× monthly maximum
lifestyle: Sleep schedule: Establish a non-negotiable bedtime of 22:30–23:00 and wake time of 07:00–07:30, aiming for 7–8 continuous hours nightly. This is critical for Yin restoration and Spirit anchoring; consistency matters more than total hours initially.

Stress management: Dedicate 20–30 minutes daily to either Tai Chi, slow walking (not brisk jogging, which depletes Yin), or gentle Qigong to decongest Liver Qi. Do not exert to heavy sweating (preserve Yin). Alternatively, seated meditation or deep belly breathing (4 counts in, 6 counts out) when stress arises at work.

Work boundaries: Set specific work-free times (e.g., no emails after 19:00, no work on weekends). If workload is fundamentally unmanageable, discuss with supervisor or consider role change; chronic stress cannot be overcome by herbs alone if the stressor persists unmodified.

Evening wind-down: Turn off all screens (phone, computer, TV) by 21:30. Instead, read, journal, or listen to gentle music. Light stretching or self-massage of the Liver-3 point (Taichong) for 1–2 minutes helps relax Qi constraint.
acupoints: Shenmen (Spirit Gate / HT7): Located on the wrist crease at the ulnar (pinky) side of the palm-side forearm, in a small depression. Place thumb on point and apply gentle sustained pressure or slow circular massage for 1–2 minutes, 1–2 times daily (especially before bed). Purpose: Primary point for calming Spirit, normalizing sleep, and treating insomnia of all types.

Taichong (Great Surge / LV3): Located on the top of the foot in the depression between the first and second metatarsal bones (between big toe and second toe). Apply firm but not painful pressure with thumb, massage in small circles for 1–2 minutes, 1–2 times daily. Purpose: Courses Liver Qi, relieves stagnation and tension, reduces irritability and anger.

Yintang (Hall of Impression / EX-HN3): Located midpoint between the eyebrows, in the space above the bridge of nose. Apply gentle circular massage with index or middle finger for 1–2 minutes, 1–2 times daily. Purpose: Calms the mind, relieves stress headache and mental agitation, supports Shen stabilization.

Zusanli (Three Mile / ST36): Located on the anterior (front) aspect of the lower leg, 3 cun (thumb-width) below the knee joint (below Dubi / ST35), one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the prominent bone ridge on the front of the shin). Apply warm pressure with thumb or warm palm 3–5 minutes, 1–2 times daily, or use mild moxa if available. Purpose: Tonifies Qi and Blood, supports constitutional Yin, strengthens overall resilience to stress.
exercise: Tai Chi (or Qigong): Practice 20–30 minutes at gentle, flowing pace, 4–5 times per week. This is ideal for coursing Liver Qi without depleting Yin; emphasize smooth movements and deep breathing. Avoid vigorous, sweating practice (saves Yin for recovery).

Gentle walking: 30–45 minutes at leisurely pace in a park or nature, early morning or early evening (avoid midday heat). Daily or 5 times per week. Do not walk to exhaustion or heavy sweating; the goal is to move Qi gently, not to build endurance.
recommendations.emotional_care: Work stress is the root cause of this acute decompensation. Emotional processing is as important as herbs: daily journaling for 10–15 minutes to externalize frustrations, or weekly discussion with a trusted friend/therapist to process work anxieties. Resentment and frustration bottled inside perpetuate Liver Qi stagnation. Set realistic expectations at work and communicate boundaries clearly to your supervisor or colleagues. Practice saying 'no' to non-essential demands. Meditation or mindfulness practice (even 10 minutes daily) helps decouple you from reactive irritability when stress arises. Consider whether your current role is sustainable long-term; if not, explore alternative work or restructuring.

herbal_formulas.name: Modified Chai Hu Long Gu Mu Li Tang (柴胡龙骨牡蛎汤加减)
ingredients: Bupleurum (Chai Hu / 柴胡) 12g
Scutellaria (Huang Qin / 黄芩) 9g
Pinellia prepared (Ban Xia / 半夏) 9g
Dragon's Bone (Long Gu / 龙骨) 15g
Oyster Shell (Mu Li / 牡蛎) 15g
Ginseng (Ren Shen / 人参 or white ginseng) 6g
Licorice (Gan Cao / 甘草) 6g
Rhubarb (Da Huang / 大黄) 6g
Half-Ripe Bitter Orange (Zhi Shi / 枳实) 9g
Sour Jujube Seed (Suan Zao Ren / 酸枣仁) 15g [ADDITION for Yin-deficiency insomnia]
Salvia Miltiorrhiza (Dan Shen / 丹参) 9g [ADDITION for Blood stasis at tongue edges and Hair Blood supply]
Spirit Poria (Fu Shen / 伏神) 9g [ADDITION for Heart Shen anchoring, replaces regular Poria]
herbal_formulas.dosage: 1 packet herbal decoction: simmer in 500 mL water for 40 minutes, then strain and divide into two doses (morning and evening with warm water, best taken 30–60 min after meals). Take for 2 weeks, then reassess with your practitioner. If good response (sleep improved, irritability reduced, face redness fading), continue for 2 additional weeks. If minimal response, modify formula or add acupuncture.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This formula simultaneously releases Liver Qi constraint (Chai Hu, Zhi Shi), anchors and calms Spirit displaced by Qi stagnation (Long Gu, Mu Li, Dan Shen, Fu Shen), and enriches Yin and Blood to cool the rising heat (Suan Zao Ren), while the cooling Scutellaria and Rhubarb clear early heat. Ginseng, Licorice, and Pinellia balance the formula's moving actions and support Spleen. This is the acute/short-term formula designed for the first 4 weeks.

herbal_formulas.name: Modified Zuo Gui Yin (左归饮加减)
ingredients: Rehmannia cooked (Shu Di Huang / 熟地黄) 12g
Goji Lycium Fruit (Gou Qi Zi / 枸杞子) 9g
Dodder Seed (Tu Si Zi / 兔丝子) 9g
Eucommia bark (Du Zhong / 杜仲) 9g
Dioscorea (Shan Yao / 山药) 9g
Licorice (Gan Cao / 甘草) 6g
Sour Jujube Seed (Suan Zao Ren / 酸枣仁) 12g [ADDITION for continued Shen support]
Biota Seed (Bai Zi Ren / 柏子仁) 9g [ADDITION for Yin nourishment and sleep]
Spirit Poria (Fu Shen / 伏神) 9g [ADDITION for Heart Shen]
herbal_formulas.dosage: 1 packet herbal decoction: simmer in 500 mL water for 40 minutes, strain, divide into two doses (morning and evening with warm water, 30–60 min after meals). Begin Week 4 after initial Chai Hu Long Gu formula, continue for 4–8 weeks. This is gentler and more tonifying, suitable for rebuilding Yin and Blood. Take for at least 6–8 weeks for durable effect.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This is the medium- and long-term formula designed to enrich Kidney Yin and Liver Blood, restore constitutional reserves, and sustain Spirit calm. Rehmannia and Goji are the core Yin and Blood tonifiers; Dioscorea and Tu Si Zi provide essence and Yin supplementation; Eucommia stabilizes Kidney function; Suan Zao Ren and Biota continue Shen support. Less moving/releasing than the acute formula, this is more nourishing and is intended to prevent relapse as stress tolerance improves.

warning_signs: Sudden rapid spreading of bald patches over multiple body sites (including eyebrows, beard, body hair): this may indicate secondary skin infection, fungal ringworm (tinea), or atypical autoimmune process requiring dermatology assessment and possible topical/systemic treatment
High fever (≥38.5 °C) concurrent with new or worsening hair loss: suggests systemic infection or inflammation, requires immediate medical evaluation and standard blood work (CBC, ESR, CMP)
Suicidal ideation or severe depression: work stress may be manifesting psychiatrically; this requires mental health professional consultation, not TCM alone
Chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations with dizziness or fainting: rule out cardiac arrhythmia or ischemia via ECG and cardiology review before attributing to Qi stagnation
Persistent bloody stools or black tarry stools: indicates GI bleeding, not a result of this TCM pattern; requires gastroenterology evaluation
Uncontrolled high blood pressure (≥180/110 mmHg): some warming herbs in this formula could theoretically raise BP; obtain baseline BP before herbal therapy
contraindications: Do NOT use heating/warming herbs (ginger, cinnamon bark, dried ginger, or warming tonics) in high doses or for prolonged periods; this patient has Yin deficiency and heat signs, and excessive warming worsens the condition

Do NOT combine these formulas with blood-thinning medications (warfarin, dabigatran, aspirin, NSAIDs) without medical supervision, as the blood-moving herbs (Salvia Dan Shen, Rhubarb Da Huang) may interact; inform your physician and TCM practitioner of any anticoagulants
Do NOT self-treat if symptoms suddenly worsen or new systemic symptoms appear; escalate to medical doctor immediately
Do NOT restrict calories or practice extreme fasting while taking these formulas; constitutional Yin deficiency requires adequate nutrition for herbs to rebuild reserves
precautions.special_notes: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune-inflammatory condition in conventional medicine. While TCM addresses the Qi-Blood-Yin substrate, a dermatology baseline is prudent to rule out secondary bacterial infection (impetigo, folliculitis) or fungal ringworm, which would require topical antibiotic or antifungal cream. If any pustules, oozing, or malodor is present at bald patches, seek dermatology urgently. Hair regrowth in alopecia areata (whether treated with TCM, topical steroids, or immunosuppressants) typically takes 8–12 weeks minimum; fine white/vellus hairs appearing at Week 4–6 are a positive sign of recovery. Do not expect dense terminal hair regrowth for at least 12 weeks. Stress remains the primary relapse risk; sustainable improvement depends on addressing the root cause (work environment, emotional resilience, lifestyle) in parallel with herbal therapy. If this is the second or third recurrence of alopecia, consider referral for acupuncture (needle therapy) as adjunct to herbs, as this pattern may require dual modality for durability.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess after 2 weeks of herbal therapy (Week 2). If insomnia improved by 1–2 hours, irritability noticeably reduced, and face redness fading, continue the acute formula (Chai Hu Long Gu) for 2 additional weeks (total 4 weeks). If minimal or no change after 2 weeks, notify your TCM practitioner for formula modification or consider adding acupuncture needle therapy. Transition to medium-term formula (Zuo Gui Yin) at Week 4. Subsequent follow-ups at Week 6 and Week 10 to monitor hair regrowth (fine/vellus hair by Week 6 is normal), sleep duration, and stress level.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1–2: Irritability and rage begin to ease; chest/rib tightness slightly looser; sleep may improve by 30–60 minutes (even modest gains are meaningful). Week 2–4: Sleep normalized to 6–7 hours; face redness noticeably faded; mood stabilized. Week 4–8: Sleep sustained at 7–8 hours; fine/white hair regrowth appears at bald patches (this is vellus/immature hair, normal first stage); face clear of redness; irritability minimal. Week 8–12: Durable sleep; progressive thickening and darkening of new hair; return to baseline emotional resilience; ability to manage work stress without acute relapse.
follow_up.next_steps: 1. Begin herbal formula immediately (Chai Hu Long Gu Mu Li Tang). 2. Establish sleep and stress management practices concurrently (Tai Chi, meditation, work boundaries). 3. Schedule follow-up with your TCM practitioner at Week 2 for pulse/tongue reassessment. 4. If insomnia persists or worsens after 2 weeks, book acupuncture (needle therapy) with a licensed acupuncturist as adjunct; acupuncture often more effective than acupressure for acute Shen disturbance. 5. Dermatology consultation to baseline alopecia areata and rule out secondary infection; inform dermatologist you are using herbal therapy and ask if topical corticosteroid or intralesional injection might accelerate regrowth (TCM and conventional dermatology can be complementary). 6. At Week 4, transition to the medium-term formula (Zuo Gui Yin) and commit to 6–8 weeks of continuous therapy for lasting constitutional rebuilding. 7. Revisit work situation and stress management; if workload remains unsustainable, escalate decision to change role or employer to ensure relapse does not occur.

parsed.disclaimer: Traditional Chinese Medicine is a complementary system of care and is not intended to replace conventional medical diagnosis or treatment. This TCM assessment is based on a partial examination (limited by remote, text-based data collection) and should not be interpreted as a definitive diagnosis. Hair loss (alopecia areata) can have multiple etiologies—autoimmune, infectious, nutritional, hormonal—and a dermatology evaluation is strongly recommended to rule out secondary conditions requiring topical or systemic medical treatment. If you experience warning signs listed above, consult a physician immediately. Use of herbal formulas should be supervised by a licensed TCM practitioner or herbalist; this report provides guidance only and is not a substitute for in-person clinical assessment. Herbal remedies may interact with medications; inform your doctor and TCM practitioner of all supplements and medicines you are taking. Constitutional and lifestyle recommendations are supportive measures and work best in conjunction with both herbal therapy and professional stress management. Individual results vary; this prognosis is based on adherence to recommendations and absence of uncontrolled comorbidities.

data.wen_inquiry: Chief complaint: Sudden patchy hair loss on top of the head (alopecia areata), recurrence after a stressful period at work. Symptoms: face redness; sleeps under six hours a night; thirst; hot flashes; excessive sweating; rage/irritability after months of work stress; tight abdomen with fullness in chest and rib-sides.
